name: Nehemiah

seo.title: Nehemiah in the Bible: the cupbearer who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall
seo.description: Nehemiah in plain words: the king's cupbearer, the night ride round the ruins, the wall built in 52 days, the Law read at the Water Gate, and his prayers.

band.lede: The king's cupbearer who wept for a ruined city. He rode round its broken walls by night, then rebuilt them in 52 days, every builder with a sword at his side.

picture.alt: A painting of a bearded man in a dark turban and a deep blue cloak over a green patterned robe, riding a grey horse at dusk. Behind him broken walls and gateways glow orange under a stormy sky, and other men stand among the ruins.

card.line: The Persian king's cupbearer, who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem in 52 days.

who: Nehemiah was a Jew at the Persian court, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes. When he heard that Jerusalem's wall lay in ruins, he wept and prayed, then asked the king to send him. As governor of Judah he rebuilt the wall in 52 days, through mockery and plots, and stood beside Ezra when the Law was read.

lines: He never took the governor's food

numbers.chip: Jews and officials at his table
lines: One ox and six sheep a day
His book ends on the fourth

tidbits.text: Chapter 3 walks right round the city, gate by gate. It names **ten gates**, from the Sheep Gate back to the Sheep Gate, and who built each stretch in between.
2 Maccabees says he founded a **library**. He gathered “the books about the kings and prophets, and the writings of David”.
Josephus tells it differently. In his *Antiquities* the wall takes **two years and four months**, and the king is Xerxes.

cite.text: Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 11, chapter 5

facts.label: Home
facts.text: The **citadel of Susa**, at the Persian court. His fathers were buried in **Jerusalem**, “the city where my fathers are buried”.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: The son of **Hacaliah**. His brother **Hanani** brought him the news from Judah.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: **Cupbearer** to King **Artaxerxes** of Persia. Then **governor** of Judah for twelve years.

facts.label: When
facts.text: The king's twentieth year: **445 or 444 BC**, the date the OCA gives.

facts.label: Title
facts.text: **Tirshatha**, in the Hebrew of 8:9 and 10:1: a Persian title for a governor. It may mean “His Excellency”. The King James Version keeps the word.

facts.label: His enemies
facts.text: **Sanballat** the Horonite, **Tobiah** the Ammonite official and **Geshem** the Arab.

facts.label: His book
facts.text: The **Book of Nehemiah**, much of it told by him, as “I”. The Hebrew Bible counts it as one book with **Ezra**.

facts.label: The covenant
facts.text: His name heads the list of those who sealed the people's covenant: “Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah”.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Nehemias**, in Latin. Older Catholic Bibles call his book the **Second Book of Esdras**.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: The Bible does not say. Josephus says he lived to “a great age”.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Most often as the **cupbearer**, handing the king his cup, as in the Urbino Bible here. Doré engraved his ride round the ruins, and Tissot painted it.

said.lede: Scripture, his enemies, a Jewish historian and two Latin writers, in their own words.

quotes.q: Also of Nehemiah the memory is great. He raised up for us fallen walls, set up the gates and bars, and rebuilt our houses.
quotes.who: The book of Sirach, in its praise of Israel's great men. It names Nehemiah, but not Ezra.

quotes.q: It is reported among the nations—and Geshem agrees—that you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall. According to these reports, you are to become their king
quotes.who: Sanballat, in an open letter sent by his servant. Nehemiah answered that he was inventing it.

quotes.q: He was a man of a good and righteous disposition, and very ambitious to make his own nation happy; and he hath left the walls of Jerusalem as an eternal monument for himself.

cite.text: Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 11, chapter 5

quotes.q: Ezra and Nehemiah, that is the Lord's helper and His consoler, are united in a single book. They restore the Temple and build up the walls of the city.
quotes.who: Jerome, in 394, in a letter to Paulinus of Nola on how to read the Bible

quotes.q: But Nehemiah, having stationed guards against those making assaults upon the people, was in no degree alarmed, and carried out what he had begun.
quotes.who: Sulpicius Severus, the friend and biographer of Martin of Tours, retelling the Bible's history

moments.title: News from Jerusalem
moments.text: Nehemiah served the Persian king in the citadel of Susa. His brother Hanani came with men from Judah, and Nehemiah asked them about the Jews who had survived the exile, and about Jerusalem. “The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.” When he heard it, he sat down and wept. “I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven.” His prayer is further down this page.

moments.title: The king's cup
moments.text: Four months later he was serving wine to King Artaxerxes. He had never been sad in front of the king, and the king saw it at once. “Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart.” Nehemiah was “overwhelmed with fear”. He said the city of his fathers lay in ruins. “What is your request?” asked the king. “So I prayed to the God of heaven and answered the king.” He asked to be sent to rebuild it. The king, “with the queen seated beside him”, asked how long he would be gone. Nehemiah named a time, and asked for letters and timber too. The king granted it all.

moments.title: The night ride
moments.text: The king sent army officers and horsemen with him. In Jerusalem he waited three days. Then he went out at night with a few men, and told no one what God had laid on his heart. “The only animal with me was the one on which I was riding.” He rode out by the Valley Gate and looked at the broken walls and the burned gates. At the King's Pool the rubble left no room for his animal to pass. So he went up the valley in the dark and looked at the wall from there. “The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing.”

moments.title: Every family a stretch of wall
moments.text: Then he spoke to the priests, the nobles and the officials. “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” He told them how the hand of God had been on him, and what the king had said. “Let us start rebuilding,” they replied. His book lists who built each part. The high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate. Goldsmiths and perfumers took their stretches. Shallum, ruler of a half-district of Jerusalem, built his “with the help of his daughters”. Priests repaired the wall in front of their own houses. Only the nobles of Tekoa “did not put their shoulders to the work”.

moments.title: A sword at every side
moments.text: Sanballat laughed at the “feeble Jews”. Tobiah joked that a fox could knock their wall down. When the wall reached half its height, they plotted an attack. Nehemiah prayed and set a guard day and night. He placed families behind the low places with swords, spears and bows. “Do not be afraid of them,” he told them. From then on half his men worked and half stood guard. The trumpeter stayed beside him, to call everyone to the place of attack. At night, he writes, “neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes”.

moments.title: The cry of the poor
moments.text: Then a great outcry rose from the people against their own kin. To buy grain in the famine they had mortgaged their fields and vineyards. Some of their daughters were already slaves. Nehemiah was “extremely angry”. He called a large assembly and faced the nobles and officials. “You are exacting usury from your own brothers!” They had nothing to say. He told them to give back the fields, vineyards and houses at once, and they swore to do it. Then he shook out the folds of his robe. “May God likewise shake out of his house and possessions every man who does not keep this promise.” The whole assembly said, “Amen.”

moments.title: Four invitations and a trap
moments.text: With only the doors of the gates left to hang, Sanballat and Geshem asked him to meet them on the plain of Ono. “But they were planning to harm me.” He said no four times. The fifth message came as an open letter, saying he meant to make himself king. “There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading,” he replied. Then a man named Shemaiah told him to hide inside the temple, because killers were coming that night. Nehemiah saw that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. “Should a man like me run away?”

moments.title: Fifty-two days
moments.text: “So the wall was completed in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul.” When their enemies heard, all the nations around them “were afraid and disheartened, for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God.” Nehemiah set the doors in the gates and put his brother Hanani in charge of the city. He told the guards not to open the gates each morning “until the sun is hot”.

moments.title: The Law read aloud
moments.text: All the people gathered in the square before the Water Gate. Ezra the scribe stood on a high wooden platform and read the Law of Moses aloud, from daybreak until noon. When he opened the book, all the people stood up. The Levites explained it so that all could understand, and the people wept as they heard it. Nehemiah the governor, Ezra and the Levites told them, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” They sent them home to feast. Then the city kept the Feast of Booths, in shelters of branches on the rooftops. “From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this.”

moments.title: Two choirs on the wall
moments.text: For the dedication, the Levites and singers came in from their villages with cymbals, harps and lyres. Nehemiah brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall and set two great choirs of thanksgiving on it. One went to the right, with Ezra leading. Nehemiah followed the other to the left. The two met in the house of God. “The women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar.”

moments.title: Tobiah's room
moments.text: In the king's thirty-second year he went back to Artaxerxes. When he returned, he found that a priest had given Tobiah a large room in the temple courts, where the offerings used to be kept. “I was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room.” The Levites had gone home to their fields, unpaid, and he brought them back. He shut the city gates for the Sabbath and warned off the traders camped outside the wall. He found men married to women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab whose children could not speak the language of Judah. He rebuked them, beat some and pulled out their hair.

miracles.lede: His own book tells no miracle. 2 Maccabees, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, tells one from his time. It comes in a letter from the Jews of Jerusalem to the Jews in Egypt.

pledge.q: remember the fire which was given when Nehemiah offered sacrifices, after he had built both the temple and the altar

more.title: Fire from a dry well
more.text: Before the exile, the letter says, godly priests hid some of the altar's fire in a dry well. Years later Nehemiah sent their descendants to find it. They found no fire, only a thick liquid. He had the priests sprinkle it on the wood and the sacrifice. Then they waited.
more.quote: and the sun shone out, which before was hidden with clouds, a great blaze was kindled, so that all men marveled.

more.title: A flame on the stones
more.text: The priests prayed while the sacrifice burned. Then Nehemiah had the rest of the liquid poured on large stones. The king of Persia heard of it, fenced the place off and made it holy. Nehemiah's men called the liquid Nephthar, which means “Cleansing”.
more.quote: When this was done, a flame was kindled; but when the light from the altar shone back, it went out.

doubt.title: Which Bibles hold it
doubt.text: 2 Maccabees is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Protestant Bibles leave it out, or print it among the Apocrypha. Ambrose of Milan retold the story for his clergy, and saw in it a picture of baptism and the Holy Spirit.

cites.text: Ambrose, *On the Duties of the Clergy*, Book 3, chapters 17 and 18

words.note: Much of his book is told in his own voice, as “I”. Outside the quiz's own section, Bible lines on this page are from the Berean Standard Bible. Sirach and 2 Maccabees, which it does not include, are from the World English Bible.

feature.kicker: When his enemies asked him to come down and talk
feature.q: I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?
feature.ctx: Sanballat and Geshem wanted to meet him on the plain of Ono. Four times they sent, and four times he gave this answer.

quotes.q: Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?
quotes.who: To the king, who had asked why his face was sad.

quotes.q: The God of heaven is the One Who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.
quotes.who: To Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, who mocked the builders.

quotes.q: Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, Who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.
quotes.who: To the builders, when an attack was expected.

quotes.q: What you are doing is not right. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?
quotes.who: To the nobles who were lending to the poor at interest.

quotes.q: Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!
quotes.who: To Shemaiah, who told him to hide in the temple.

quotes.q: Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
quotes.who: To the people weeping at the reading of the Law. Many translations have only “Then he said”, after a verse that names Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites together. The Berean Standard Bible names Nehemiah.

myths.claim: The builders worked with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other.
myths.truth: Nehemiah 4 tells of three groups. Half of his own men stood guard with spears, shields and bows. Those who carried loads “worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.” The builders needed both hands, so each worked “with his sword strapped at his side.” No trowel is named. Josephus tells it the same way: “the mason had his sword on, as well as he that brought the materials”.

cite.text: Nehemiah 4:16-18; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 11, chapter 5

myths.truth: His own book is about the wall and its gates. By the Book of Ezra, the Temple had been finished long before, “in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius.” Two later writers say more. 2 Maccabees speaks of the fire given when Nehemiah sacrificed, “after he had built both the temple and the altar”. In Josephus he asks the king for leave “to finish the building of the temple”.

cite.text: Ezra 6:15; 2 Maccabees 1:18; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 11, chapter 5

myths.claim: His Catholic feast day is 13 July.
myths.truth: A German dictionary of saints of 1875 does list him under 13 July, but only to say he has no feast. On that day the Bollandists, the Jesuit editors of the lives of the saints, passed Nehemiah over, because he was not venerated. The *Roman Martyrology* of 1916 has no entry for him, and neither does its 2004 edition. In both, 13 July is the day of Ezra.

circle.name: Hanani
circle.text: One of his brothers. He brought the news that the wall was down. Later Nehemiah put him in charge of Jerusalem.

circle.name: Artaxerxes
circle.text: The Persian king he served. He noticed the sad face, and gave him leave, letters, timber and an escort. He made him governor of Judah.

circle.name: Ezra
circle.text: The priest and scribe who read the Law to the people at the Water Gate, with Nehemiah the governor beside him. At the dedication he led one of the two choirs along the wall.

circle.name: Hananiah
circle.text: Commander of the fortress. Nehemiah put him in charge of Jerusalem with Hanani, “because he was a faithful man who feared God more than most.”

circle.name: Sanballat the Horonite
circle.text: His chief enemy. He mocked the builders, plotted an attack and spread the rumour that Nehemiah meant to be king. A grandson of the high priest married his daughter, and Nehemiah drove the young man away.

circle.name: Tobiah the Ammonite
circle.text: Sanballat's ally, with friends among the nobles of Judah. He wrote letters to frighten Nehemiah. Later he moved into a room in the temple, until Nehemiah threw his things out.

circle.name: Geshem the Arab
circle.text: The third of his enemies. He joined the mocking, and the open letter named him as the source of the rumour of revolt.

circle.name: Shemaiah son of Delaiah
circle.text: A prophet hired by Tobiah and Sanballat. He urged Nehemiah to hide in the temple, so that he would sin and lose his good name.

death.title: How his story ends
death.big: The Bible does not say how or when he died. His book simply stops, on a prayer.
paras: His book ends on his second stay in Jerusalem. He set the priests and Levites to their duties, and arranged for wood for the altar and for the firstfruits. Then he wrote his last line.
Josephus, writing about 93, gives the only account of his end: “he came to a great age, and then died.”

items.k: The last words of his book
items.q: Remember me, O my God, with favor.
items.ctx: The fourth time he prays it. The first came after his twelve years as governor: “Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people.”

saint.big: The Orthodox honour him as a saint, the **Prophet Nehemiah**, on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers. He has no day in the Catholic calendar, and Protestant churches keep none.

churches.note: Sunday of the Forefathers, in December
His prayer is read on a Lutheran day of penitence

paras: The OCA lists the **Prophet Nehemiah** on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers, the Sunday between 11 and 17 December. The Russian calendar *Azbuka Very* keeps him on the same Sunday, so his day moves each year.
Ambrose of Milan calls him “holy Nehemiah”. The *Roman Martyrology* gives him no day: see Often misquoted, above.
Lutherans of the ELCA read his prayer from Nehemiah 1 on their Day of Penitence.

prayer.title: His prayer in Susa
prayer.intro: When the news came, he wept, fasted and prayed for days. His prayer confesses the sins of Israel, his own family's among them. It holds God to His promise to Moses to gather the scattered. It ends with a request about the king:
prayer.q: O Lord, may Your ear be attentive to my prayer and to the prayers of Your servants who delight to revere Your name. Give Your servant success this day, I pray, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.

kin.name: Esther
kin.text: Another Jew at the Persian court in the citadel of Susa. She too went before the king for her people: “And if I perish, I perish!”

kin.name: Daniel
kin.text: A Jew who served foreign kings. He prayed three times a day at windows that “opened toward Jerusalem”.

kin.name: Joseph
kin.text: A Hebrew raised high in a foreign court, who used it to save his people: “God sent me before you to preserve you as a remnant on the earth”.
